record.original_question: If a graph admits a thrackle drawing, must it have at most as many edges as vertices?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 2.7 If a graph can be thrackled, then the number of edges does not exceed the number of vertices.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A drawing of a simple graph $G$ in the plane is called a *thrackle drawing* if every edge is drawn as a simple (Jordan) arc, any two edges meet in exactly one point (which is either a common endpoint or a proper transversal crossing), and no two edges share more than one point. A graph is said to be *thrackleable* if it admits a thrackle drawing.

Prove or disprove the following: every thrackleable graph $G$ on $n$ vertices satisfies
$$|E(G)| \le |V(G)| = n.$$
artifact.status_search_result: Conway's thrackle conjecture remains open. The best known upper bounds are linear in n but strictly larger than n: Fulek–Pach gave roughly 1.428n, improved by Goddyn–Xu to about 1.4n, then to ~1.393n by Xu, and a recent bound around 1.3984n has been announced. The conjectured equality |E| ≤ n has not been established in general.

status_evidence.title: Thrackle - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Conway's thrackle conjecture states that a thrackle has at most as many edges as vertices; it remains open.

status_evidence.title: On the Bounds of Conway's Thrackles
status_evidence.snippet: Improves the upper bound on the number of edges of a thrackleable graph.
status_evidence.claim: Best known bounds are linear, e.g. ~1.4n, exceeding the conjectured n.

status_evidence.title: A computational approach to Conway's thrackle conjecture
status_evidence.snippet: Fulek–Pach approach yielding linear upper bounds.
status_evidence.claim: Progress toward but not resolution of the conjecture.
